opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first thing I'd want to create is a lot more free time for people. That sounds a little abstract, but think about how much of our lives goes to tasks that aren't really "us": folding laundry, cleaning, moving things from one place to another, the repetitive physical labor that keeps a household or a factory running. If robots can genuinely take that over, I think the most valuable thing they create isn't the robot itself, it's the hours they give back.

On a more personal level, I'd love to build something like a home companion that really understands the physical world. Not just a voice assistant that can tell you the weather, but something that can see your kitchen is a mess, know where everything goes, and help an elderly parent get up safely in the morning. Physical intelligence in everyday spaces is still so far behind digital intelligence. We have models that can write essays, but almost nothing that can reliably tidy a messy room. Closing that gap feels like one of the most meaningful things I could work on.

And then, maybe a bit more dreamy: once robots are capable enough, I'd want to see them open up creation itself. Imagine anyone who has an idea for a product, a piece of furniture, a small business, being able to just describe it and have robots help prototype and build it. Today, making physical things requires capital, factories, and specialized skills. If robots lower that barrier the way software lowered the barrier for building apps, I think we'd see an explosion of creativity in the physical world. That's the future I find most exciting.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses creating free time, a home companion, and lowering barriers to physical creation. It does not express interest in discovering whether stories matching Kay Ke’s tastes appeal to others.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing I'd want to make isn't a product, it's a kind of freedom. When people ask what I'd build once robots really work, they expect me to say a humanoid that does your laundry or a warehouse that runs itself. Those are fine. But I think the deeper answer is that I'd want to create time for people.

Think about what most of us actually spend our days on. It's not the things we'd choose. It's the moving, lifting, sorting, cleaning, waiting, repeating. If a machine can genuinely take that on, not in a demo but in the messy real world, then what you've created is a few hours a day handed back to every person. What they do with it is their business. Some will rest, some will learn something, some will just spend more time with their kids. I find that more exciting than any single robot.

The second thing, and this is more personal, is I'd want to build robots for the places that are too dangerous or too thankless for people. Mines, disaster zones, deep sea, elder care at three in the morning. These are the jobs where the shortage isn't about wages, it's that nobody should have to do them in the current form. If we can put a capable machine in there, we're not replacing someone, we're relieving them.

And then there's the part I'm almost shy to say out loud. Once robots can move through the world and learn from it, they become a new kind of scientific instrument. A lab that runs experiments around the clock, a fleet that explores somewhere humans can't easily go. I'd love to see what we discover when physical experimentation stops being bottlenecked by human hands.

So if I had to compress it: I'd want to create a world where the physical drudgery is optional, the dangerous work is done by something that can't be hurt, and curiosity has more hands than it does today. The robots are just the means. The thing I actually want to build is the world on the other side of them.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses creating time, safer work, and scientific discovery with robots. It does not express interest in finding out whether stories that match Kay Ke’s tastes appeal to other people.
